newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Troubled Belarus, in key location, worries West.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Belarus, in key location, worries West.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
The turmoil in Belarus threatens to cause fresh problems for Russia, NATO and others at a time when crucial decisions are due on how to deal with a "grey zone" of security in Eastern Europe.

Diplomats say this is reflected in growing Western concern about the power struggle between President Alexander Lukashenko and his parliament. There are also worries about the fate of former Soviet nuclear weapons still held by Belarus.
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, the United States and its allies have paid little attention to the former Soviet republic of 10 million people.

But that is changing as NATO approaches decisions next year on which countries from the old communist bloc can join as new members, and which will be left out for now. Belarus shares borders with countries that are involved in this process.
While some East European countries like Poland are clear candidates to join Western institutions soon, others like Russia, Ukraine and Belarus are not -- and resent it.
"This is a crisis right on the faultline between East and West and it could have repercussions beyond the borders of Belarus," said one senior European diplomat.
"We have a very delicate process ahead of us and if Belarus goes really bad, it will complicate things."
Belarus, like Russia, is deeply opposed to NATO expansion and has hinted it may keep 18 former Soviet SS-25 intercontinental nuclear missiles on its territory in protest.

Under international agreements, the weapons are supposed to be transferred to Russia before the end of the year. While Belarus could not launch the missiles, Western diplomats say they could be used as a "bargaining chip" and to play on existing security fears in Poland or the Baltic states.
Poland has already called for calm and restraint in its troubled neighbour and diplomats say European countries may now offer to mediate in the political crisis.
Apart from the war in former Yugoslavia, attempts to keep the lid on potential conflicts in Central and Eastern Europe so far have borne some fruit.
The 15-nation EU and the Vienna-based Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) have helped broker agreements on minority rights and other sensitive issues.

But diplomats admit mediation in Belarus could be difficult. Western capitals have made clear they regard Lukashenko as a maverick and have effectively backed the parliament, where critics accuse him of dictatorial tendencies.
The United States expressed its concern again on Monday, saying there was no apparent legal basis for Lukashenko to take more power for himself by seeking to change the constitution.
German parliamentarian Karsten Voigt, speaking at a meeting of parliamentarians from NATO countries in Paris, said the president's behaviour was "illegal, non-democratic and sometimes...crazy".
Diplomats say Russia -- the major player in the region -- seems neither able or willing to get involved so far.
Still smarting from the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia has talked of political and economic union with Belarus but there is little real will in Moscow to proceed with it.
"The Russians have enough problems of their own, but their hand could be forced if there is a real breakdown," said another diplomat. "That is another headache for us."
Belarus also shares a border with two Baltic republics, Latvia and Lithuania, as well as with Poland and Ukraine.
Despite NATO's pledge that expansion into Eastern Europe will improve security for all, the process of enlargement will be fraught with difficulty in this region.
Unrest in Belarus would increase the pressure on NATO from Poland and the Baltic republics to open its doors soon, while adding to resentment in Russia and Ukraine.
Russia is opposed to NATO expansion and Ukraine is also uneasy, fearing that it will be left out in the cold.

The Baltic republics want to be among the first to join NATO but are unlikely to make it. Diplomats say Poland, along with the Czech republic, Hungary and possibly Slovenia are the front-runners to join NATO.
